question: What is the most common antimetabolite used to treat uveitis in children?
explanation: Azathioprine, methotrexate, and mycophenolate mofetil are all antimetabolites that can be used to treat uveitis in children. Methotrexate is most commonly used, and numerous studies have shown its eﬃcacy in treating both arthritis and uveitis in children. Etanercept is not an antimetabolite. It is a TNF-alpha inhibitor that should be avoided in the treatment of uveitis because it may cause inﬂammatory ocular disease.

question: What maternal disorder has been associated with segmental fetal optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH)?
explanation: Segmental optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH) may be associated with maternal diabetes mellitus. ONH is characterized by a decrease in the number of optic nerve axons. The disc is small, pale or grey, and is classically associated with a yellow-to-white ring around the disc (double ring sign). It may be unilateral or bilateral and is often asymmetric. Patients with ONH are at risk for midline central nervous system anomalies, including absence of the septum pellucidum and agenesis of the corpus callosum, as well as other cerebral hemisphere and pituitary gland abnormalities. Thus, an associated seizure disorder and hypothyroidism may be present. ONH has been associated with fetal alcohol syndrome and maternal ingestion of phenytoin, quinine, and LSD.

question: Wilms tumor may develop in 30 to 50 of children with what congenital disorder?
explanation: Sporadic aniridia is associated with the WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and mental retardation). Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is usually autosomal dominant, and 50% of cases develop glaucoma. Ocular ﬁndings in Goldenhar syndrome can include Duane syndrome, microphthalmia, upper eyelid coloboma, iris abnormalities, and corneal hypoesthesia. Weill-Marchesani syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant disease. Its ocular manifestations include microspherophakic lenses, severe myopia, and ectopia lentis.

question: What is the best test of binocular alignment to identify the presence of a tropia?
explanation: Cover-uncover testing is the most important test to reveal a tropia. Alternate cover testing will measure both a tropia and a phoria. Worth 4-dot testing best measures suppression. The Lancaster red-green test is used for incomitant strabismus. Double Maddox rod testing precludes fusion and therefore does not diﬀerentiate between heterophorias and heterotropias.

question: The greatest risk of rebleeding in traumatic hyphema occurs how long after initial injury?
explanation: One of the risks of hyphema is rebleeding, with worsening symptoms. This is especially critical in children, who often are noncompliant with activity restrictions. The greatest risk for rebleeding occurs within 3 to 7 days. After 7 days, the risk progressively decreases.

question: A 12-year-old boy is diagnosed with well-controlled, intermittent exotropia. What is stereopsis testing most likely to reveal?

explanation: Intermittent exotropia is an outward deviation that becomes manifest during times of visual inattention, fatigue, or stress. In the early stages of the disorder, the deviation is usually larger for distance viewing than for near. Thus, sensory testing at near is typically excellent, including stereopsis and fusion on Worth 4 Dot testing. When the eye deviates, suppression of the image typically occurs, rather than the recognition of diplopia.

question: An ophthalmologist examines a 3- month-old child born at full term to a mother who was diagnosed with rubella during the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy. What would the most likely ﬁnding be?

The syndrome includes a peculiar nuclear cataract that is sometimes ﬂoating in liquiﬁed cortex, as well as glaucoma, microphthalmos, and retinopathy (salt-and-pepper fundus). Retinopathy is the most common ﬁnding. Sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, and developmental delay are other systemic manifestations. Choroiditis and uveitis are typically seen in toxoplasmosis or cytomegalovirus infections. Bilateral interstitial keratitis is found in approximately 10% of older children and adults with congenital syphilis. Bitot spots are seen in vitamin A deﬁciency.

question: What is the most common ocular manifestation of abusive head trauma?
explanation: The most common ocular manifestation of abusive head trauma (AHT), present in approximately 80% of cases, is retinal hemorrhage. These hemorrhages can be seen in all layers of the retina and may be unilateral or bilateral. They are found most commonly in the posterior pole but can also be present peripherally. question: After attempted but unsuccessful treatment of his convergence insuﬃciency with orthoptic exercises, a 35-year-old man is unwilling to try adding prism to his glasses. What surgical procedure is most likely to improve his function?

explanation: Surgical treatment of convergence insuﬃciency is intended to improve ocular alignment primarily at near with reduction of the patient's exodeviation. This can be accomplished by lateral rectus recession or medial rectus resection, with no strong data suggesting one procedure is better, but medial rectus resection is more commonly chosen. Anterior transposition of the inferior oblique muscle can be used to treat dissociated vertical deviation. Recession/resection of all 4 rectus muscles can be used to treat congenital nystagmus in some patients. Posterior ﬁxation of the lateral rectus muscles can be used for improvement of strabismus in high myopes.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the eye clinic for an annual examination. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/25 in her right eye and 20/20 in her left eye. explanation: The ﬁgure demonstrates vertical-oblique breaks in Descemet membrane. This presentation is most consistent with forceps delivery. question: In congenital nasolacrimal obstruction, what is the most common blockage location?
explanation: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction typically occurs at the most distal portion of the lacrimal duct due to incomplete canalization near full- term gestation (40 weeks) of what was a solid structure in the fetus. This blockage occurs at the valve of Hasner. The canaliculi and puncta as well as the valve of Rosenmüller, which is in the region of the junction of the canaliculi, are more likely to have canalized normally.

question: What is the inheritance pattern of ectopia lentis et pupillae?

question: What optic nerve ﬁnding is most characteristic of dominant optic atrophy?

explanation: Dominant optic atrophy typically presents before age 10, with visual acuity ranging from 20/40 to 20/100. question: An 8-year-old patient presents with lethargy, bilateral vision loss, bilateral pain with eye movement, and swollen optic discs. Her neurologic examination is normal, and aside from optic nerve enhancement, the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) result is normal as well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Optic neuritis is a demyelinating disorder of the optic nerve, usually considered to be autoimmune. In children, it usually presents after a viral illness. Optic neuritis in children, in contrast with that in adults, is more frequently bilateral and associated with disc edema, as well as vision loss, systemic symptoms, and pain on eye movement. Although multiple sclerosis can present with optic neuritis, the diagnosis requires brain lesions on MRI. Increased intracranial pressure and compressive optic neuropathy can present with vision loss and swollen optic discs, but typically do not involve pain with eye movements.

question: The 3-step test for cyclovertical muscle function is a useful diagnostic test for what class of vertical strabismus?

question: Orbital cellulitis in a 7-year-old patient most commonly arises from where?
explanation: Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a 7-year-old patient, the maxillary and frontal sinuses are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. Other causative factors include the thinness of the lamina papyracea and venous drainage from the ethmoid sinus to the orbit. In adults, infections are usually polymicrobial, including gram- positive cocci, Moraxella, and H. inﬂuenzae. However, in children, the causative agent is usually a single organism that is typically a gram- positive organism. Adults often require early surgical intervention, while children typically improve with intravenous antibiotics alone.

question: In a patient with ocular toxoplasmosis, what physical examination ﬁnding should prompt HIV testing?
explanation: Toxoplasmosis typically presents as a focal white retinitis, often adjacent to a pigmented chorioretinal scar with overlying vitritis. Multiple active lesions in one or both eyes are rare and should prompt HIV testing. HIV-positive patients have a high rate of central nervous system (CNS) involvement and should undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast. Granulomatous anterior uveitis, macular involvement, and segmental perivascular plaques can all be seen in toxoplasmosis and are not speciﬁc to the presentation of toxoplasmosis in immunocompromised individuals.

question: What clinical ﬁnding suggests a bilateral rather than a unilateral superior oblique muscle palsy?
explanation: Unilateral cases of superior oblique paresis usually show little, if any, V pattern and less than 10° of extorsion in downgaze. In contrast, bilateral cases of superior oblique paresis usually show a V pattern. Extorsion is 10° or more in downgaze; more than 15° of extorsion in primary position is highly suggestive of bilateral involvement. Subjective incyclodiplopia is common in acquired bilateral cases. The Bielschowsky head-tilt test yields positive results on tilt to each side-- that is, right head tilt produces a right hypertropia, and left head tilt produces a left hypertropia. There is bilateral oblique muscle dysfunction. Patients may exhibit a chin-down head position. Symmetric palsies may show little or no hypertropia in primary position.

question: Most commonly, orbital cellulitis is caused by the spread of the infection from where?
explanation: Orbital cellulitis is an infection of the orbit that involves the tissues posterior to the orbital septum. It is most commonly caused by the spread of infection from ethmoid or frontal sinusitis. Eyelid margin disease and insect bites can lead to lid swelling and can become secondarily infected. However, the infection is typically conﬁned to the lid anterior to the orbital septum, leading to preseptal cellulitis rather than orbital cellulitis.

question: What category of congenital anomaly is represented by a typical iris coloboma?

question: What structure maintains the position of the extraocular muscles relative to the orbit? Corneal light reﬂex tests are useful in assessing ocular alignment in patients who are unable to cooperate suﬃciently to allow cover testing or who have poor vision in one or both eyes, and consequently have poor ﬁxation. The main tests of this type are the Hirschberg, modiﬁed Krimsky, Brückner, and major amblyoscope methods. Children with good vision in both eyes will usually tolerate cover methods and do not display avoidance. The corneal light reﬂex method is less sensitive or quantitatively precise than cover-uncover or cross-cover methods, so it is less helpful in less severe amblyopia or strabismus. The Hirschberg method is based on the premise that 1 mm of decentration of the corneal light reﬂection corresponds to approximately 7°, or 15 prism diopters, of ocular deviation of the visual axis. The Krimsky method uses reﬂections produced on both corneas by a penlight and is ideally used at near ﬁxation. The original method involved placing prisms in front of the deviating eye. More common modiﬁcations today involve holding prisms before the ﬁxating eye or split between the 2 eyes. By adjusting the prisms to center the corneal reﬂection in the deviated eye, it is possible to approximate and quantitate the near deviation. In order to perform the Brückner test, the examiner uses a direct ophthalmoscope to obtain a red reﬂex simultaneously in both eyes. Note that this test detects but does not measure the deviation. The major amblyoscope method uses separate target illumination, which can be moved to center the corneal light reﬂection. The amount of deviation is then read directly from the scale of the amblyoscope.

Indications for treatment include an immunocompromised patient, dense vitreous opacity, large lesions greater than 1 disc diameter in size, multiple lesions, decreased visual acuity, frequent recurrences, or retinitis threatening the optic nerve or macula. The classic regimen for the treatment of ocular toxoplasmosis consists of triple therapy: pyrimethamine (loading dose, 50–100 mg; treatment dose, 25–50 mg/day), sulfadiazine (treatment dose, 1 g, 4 times/day), and prednisone (treatment dose, 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, depending on the severity of the inﬂammation). question: A patient presents with unilateral upper eyelid retraction on ipsilateral attempted adduction. What is the most likely cause of this ﬁnding?

options.A: aberrant regeneration of cranial nerve (CN) III

explanation: Cranial nerve III palsies displaying aberrant regeneration have a variety of clinical presentations, one of which is upper eyelid retraction on attempted adduction. Other common ﬁndings are pupillary miosis with attempted eyelid elevation, adduction, or infraduction. These ﬁndings are caused by nerve axon damage, such as compression from a slowly expanding mass in the cavernous sinus, leading to nerve ﬁber misrouting that produces several synkinetic phenomena (ie, co- contraction of muscles that normally are not activated together). Thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of upper eyelid retraction but is not triggered by adduction. Dorsal midbrain syndrome is a bilateral condition in which upper eyelid retraction (Collier sign) occurs due to compression of the posterior midbrain, but it manifests with convergence insuﬃciency and impaired upgaze, and it is not triggered by adduction. question: A 12-year-old boy presents in the spring with bilateral ocular itching. and his upper lid tarsal conjunctiva is shown in the ﬁgure. Light microscopy examination of a scraping of this conjunctiva would likely show what conﬁrmatory ﬁnding?

question: A 2-week-old infant with leukocoria is suspected of having persistent fetal vasculature (PFV). Anatomically, what globe size strongly supports a diagnosis of PFV over retinoblastoma?
explanation: Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) results from the failure of the fetal hyaloid vascular complex to regress and is almost always unilateral. question: What anatomical feature of the inferior oblique muscle diﬀers from that of the other extraocular muscles?

question: What part of the visual system demonstrates abnormal neuronal development in amblyopia?
explanation: Amblyopic visual deﬁcits result primarily from visual cortical changes. With abnormal visual experience early in life, cells of the primary visual cortex can lose their ability to respond to stimulation of 1 or both eyes, and the cells that remain responsive show signiﬁcant functional deﬁciencies, including abnormally large receptive ﬁelds. Visual cortex deﬁciencies may account for the crowding phenomenon, in which optotypes are easier to recognize when isolated than when surrounded by similar forms. question: A 4-month-old girl has a large esotropia and mild limitation to abduction of both eyes. Her examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

question: Pathologic examination of an infant's eye demonstrates multiple ocular malformations including microphthalmos, iris and ciliary body colobomas, retinal dysplasia, and an area of cartilage within the ciliary body coloboma (ﬁgure). What diagnosis is most appropriate?

question: What is the most common outcome when a needle perforates the sclera during strabismus surgery?

question: A patient undergoes a retrobulbar anesthetic injection just prior to glaucoma ﬁltering surgery. What change in eye position is the surgeon likely to observe intraoperatively?

explanation: Port-wine stain on the eyelid, choroidal hemangioma, retinal vascular tortuosity, and glaucoma are all found in encephalofacial angiomatosis (also called Sturge-Weber syndrome). However, glaucoma is the most serious ocular complication and can be quite diﬃcult to control. Encephalofacial angiomatosis consists of a facial cutaneous angioma (port-wine stain), which is composed of well-formed capillaries in the dermis and usually involves the forehead and upper eyelid. The lesion can extend to the lower eyelid and maxillary and mandibular regions and does not always conform to the distribution of the trigeminal divisions. The eye ipsilateral to the port-wine stain may have tortuous vessels and arteriovenous communications in the retina and choroidal angiomatosis (ketchup fundus). Choroidal hemangiomas are asymptomatic in childhood; however, in adolescence or adulthood, the choroid sometimes becomes markedly thickened. Degeneration or detachment of the overlying retina with severe vision loss may occur; however, this is less common than glaucoma. The likelihood of glaucoma is increased if there is involvement of the upper eyelid skin, choroidal hemangioma, iris heterochromia, and episcleral hemangioma. Other serious nonocular complications include cerebral calciﬁcations and seizures, and leptomeningeal vascular malformations ipsilateral to the skin lesion.

question: What ocular condition are curvilinear tears in Descemet membrane most often seen in?

question: What is the most common form of childhood leukemia?

Forced duction testing determines whether an ocular motility dysfunction is a restrictive or paretic process. The test is performed by ﬁrst applying topical anesthesia to the eye. question: When examining an optic nerve, what clinical ﬁnding may support a suspicion for optic disc drusen rather than true papilledema?

Disc drusen may appear as refractile gray-yellow bodies if near the surface of the nerve. However, often they are buried and not clinically visible. One useful clinical ﬁnding often seen with disc drusen is anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels over the disc. Rare complications of disc drusen include subretinal neovascular membrane or hemorrhage. B scan ultrasonography and computed tomography are useful imaging tools to identify disc drusen. question: What is the inheritance pattern for ectopia lentis et pupillae?
explanation: Ectopia lentis et pupillae is a rare, autosomal recessive condition. Pertinent clinical features include bilaterally displaced pupils, usually inferotemporally, with lens dislocation in the opposite direction of the displaced pupil. Ectopia lentis et pupillae may be the result of membranes extending from a posterior origin to attach to the proximal pupil margin. The ﬁgures show these ﬁndings. The membranes are believed to cause traction of the iris toward the membranes (resulting in the iris abnormality) and disruption of the zonules (resulting in lens subluxation in the opposite direction). Aﬀected patients have microspherophakia, miosis, and poor pupillary dilation with mydriatics. Lens dislocation causes decreased visual acuity, making spectacle correction essential. High myopia secondary to axial globe elongation has been reported. Aphakic correction is often needed, depending on the degree of lens dislocation. Amblyopia is the main complication and is managed by refractive correction and occlusion therapy. Lensectomy may result in retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage. High- frequency ultrasound preoperatively may allow assessment of risk or retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage. Ectopia lentis et pupillae is nonprogressive.

question: A 6-year-old boy with neuroblastoma is found to have acquired Horner syndrome. What is the most likely site of the causative neuroblastoma?

question: A toddler presents with ptosis and a chin-up position. What is the most important determinant in choosing the surgical technique for repair?

question: An 18-month-old child with congenital jerk-wave nystagmus has dampening of her nystagmus when she crosses her eyes. Examination reveals nystagmus with attempted abduction and a head turn with occlusion of either eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?

question: During a cover/uncover test of the right eye, the patient's right eye drifts out when covered. The left eye does not move. The right eye never drifts out under binocular conditions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

question: A 9-year-old child with a history of recurrent bacterial infections develops an intractable respiratory infection that proves fatal. The ocular and histopathologic ﬁndings of the patient are shown in the ﬁgure below. What is the most likely underlying disease in this patient?

Two notable syndromes associated with ocular-cutaneous albinism are Chédiak-Higashi syndrome and Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with a mutation in a lysosomal traﬃcking regulator protein that renders inadequate phagocytosis. This results in recurrent pyogenic infections, often involving the respiratory and cutaneous systems. Patients with Chédiak-Higashi syndrome rarely survive past 10 years of age and often succumb to infection. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by ocular-cutaneous albinism and bleeding problems from a platelet abnormality. Gaucher disease is an autosomal recessive inherited disorder of metabolism involving glucocerebroside. Gaucher disease is not associated with albinism. question: What method is recommended for assessing the refractive state in children with amblyopia?
explanation: Cycloplegic retinoscopy is the most objective and accurate method to determine the ocular refractive state in amblyopia. Due to the large accommodative capacity and tone in children, cycloplegia is necessary to accurately determine the full refractive error, especially in patients with hyperopia. Therapy for refractive amblyopia is predicated upon correcting the full refractive error of the amblyopic eye(s) and penalizing the least amblyopic or non-amblyopic eye. Because an amblyopic eye’s ability to control accommodation tends to be impaired, this eye cannot be relied on to compensate for uncorrected hyperopia as would a normal child’s eye. Retinoscopy under anesthesia (but without complete cycloplegia), manifest refraction, and autorefraction are not satisfactory, because they may not determine the full optical refractive state in the highly accommodative pediatric eye. optic nerve glioma

question: What would be the most likely ﬁndings in a 15-month-old patient diagnosed with congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome?

explanation: Congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome or congenital ﬁbrosis of the extraocular muscles (CFEOM) is a group of conditions within the general category of congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders caused by primary dysinnervation of the extraocular muscles. Congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome leads to replacement of sparsely innervated muscle by ﬁbrous tissue. Congenital ﬁbrosis syndrome must be diﬀerentiated from thyroid eye disease, myasthenia gravis, 3rd nerve palsy, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO). Thyroid eye disease would more likely present with proptosis and lid retraction with limitations of extraocular eye movements. Myasthenia gravis may present with ptosis and progressive decrease in extraocular movements, and this would be variable from day to day. Superior rectus weakness or overaction are recognized associations and contribute to causing vertical deviations. Progressive loss of extraocular movements over years would be consistent with CPEO. A third nerve palsy may present with unilateral or bilateral ptosis and limitation of adduction, along with limitation of supra- and infraduction while abduction is intact. Möbius syndrome will have facial nerve weakness, and vertical motility will be intact.
